name: Georges de La Tour
teaser: The French painter of candlelight — his nocturnal scenes of card cheats, sleeping Magdalens, and a baby Jesus lit by a single flame were forgotten for 300 years, then rediscovered in the 20th century as some of the most mysterious paintings ever made.

exploreAction.targetName: The Cheat with the Ace of Diamonds (Louvre) — the candle
exploreAction.instruction: A card game under candlelight: the cheat passes an ace behind his back while the lady of the house signals the dealer. Look at the faces — half in light, half in shadow — and the hand gestures that tell the whole story. La Tour's darkness is as precise as his light.

name: The Le Nain Brothers
teaser: Three French brothers — Antoine, Louis, and Mathieu — who painted peasants with a dignity no one had granted them before: farm families at supper, plowmen, children — still, grave, and monumental. They signed only 'Le Nain,' so no one knows who painted what.

exploreAction.targetName: The Family Meal or Peasants' Meal (Louvre) — the faces
exploreAction.instruction: A peasant family shares bread and wine in a dim kitchen. Look at the faces: not caricatures, not saints — just people, painted with the seriousness usually reserved for kings. The Le Nains gave the poor the one thing art never gave them: their own portrait.

name: Philippe de Champaigne
teaser: The Brussels-born painter who became the portraitist of 17th-century Paris — his Cardinal Richelieu glows in his famous triple portrait, and his austere Jansenist religious paintings are so plain they feel modern. He gave France its official faces.

exploreAction.targetName: The Triple Portrait of Cardinal Richelieu (National Gallery, London) — the three views
exploreAction.instruction: Three views of one man, painted so a sculptor could work from it: full face, three-quarter, and profile. Look at the absolute control of likeness — the jowls, the thin lips, the cap. Champaigne's realism was so exact it made the cardinal look almost kind.

name: Hyacinthe Rigaud
teaser: The French court painter whose Portrait of Louis XIV — the Sun King in ermine, heels, and a blue velvet coronation robe — became the most copied image of power in history. He painted Versailles's royalty and its enemies, whoever paid.

exploreAction.targetName: Portrait of Louis XIV (Louvre) — the pose
exploreAction.instruction: Louis was 63 when this was painted, but the portrait freezes him in eternal kingship: sword, crown, scepter, and a face that says 'I am the state.' Look at the ermine, the velvet, the silk — Rigaud painted fabric so richly you can hear it rustle. The most expensive image of its century.

name: François Boucher
teaser: The Rococo painter of pink clouds, shepherdesses, and goddesses with powdered hair — the favorite of Madame de Pompadour, he made French painting synonymous with pleasure. His Venus landscapes are the eighteenth century at its most delicious.

exploreAction.targetName: Diana Leaving Her Bath (Louvre) — the skin
exploreAction.instruction: The goddess of the hunt sits by a stream with her nymphs, her skin painted in layers of pearl and rose. Look at the composition: the body curves through the canvas like a wave. Boucher's world has no gravity, no work, no winter — just pleasure, eternally arranged.

name: Jean-Honoré Fragonard
teaser: The Rococo's last great painter of passion — his Swing shows a young woman flying high while a suitor spies under her skirt; his brushwork is so fast and lush it feels improvised. He outlived the taste that made him and died poor.

exploreAction.targetName: The Swing (Wallace Collection, London) — the composition
exploreAction.instruction: Everything in this painting points up: the ropes, the trees, the flying slipper, the girl's delighted kick. Look at the two men — the hidden suitor and the oblivious old bishop pushing the swing. Fragonard painted the most famous wink in art history.

name: Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin
teaser: The French painter of kitchen life who made a copper pot and a loaf of bread more moving than any battle scene — his still lifes glow with an almost religious attention, and his genre scenes of servants and children are full of quiet dignity.

exploreAction.targetName: The Silver Tureen (Louvre) — the reflections
exploreAction.instruction: A tureen, a knife, some bread, a bottle — and a universe of reflections. Look at how Chardin paints the metal's curve, the highlights, the shadow of the knife across the table. He said you don't paint with colors, you paint with feeling. Look closely: that's feeling.

name: Antoine Watteau
teaser: The French painter who invented the 'fête galante' — elegant picnics in silken parks where couples whisper and musicians play, all tinted with melancholy. His Pilgrimage to Cythera made him the toast of Paris and the most poetic painter of the Rococo.

exploreAction.targetName: The Pilgrimage to Cythera (Louvre) — the mood
exploreAction.instruction: Couples prepare to leave the island of love, their boat waiting. Look at the mood: it should be a party, but it feels like goodbye — the rose-covered statue, the turning backs, the fading light. Watteau painted pleasure with the knowledge that it ends.

name: Jean-Baptiste Greuze
teaser: The French painter of moral melodrama — his tearful scenes of virtuous daughters, dying fathers, and punished sons turned domestic virtue into a theatrical event and made him the most popular painter in 1760s France. Diderot adored him; the Academy, less so.

exploreAction.targetName: The Village Bride (Louvre) — the tears
exploreAction.instruction: A peasant wedding contract is signed while the bride's mother weeps and her little brother tugs her skirt. Look at the staging: every gesture explains itself, like actors hitting marks. Greuze painted sermons; whether you cry or laugh at them is your business.

name: Hubert Robert
teaser: The French painter of ruins and gardens — his imaginary landscapes of broken Roman temples, hanging gardens, and flooded galleries made decay look delightful. He also helped design the gardens of Versailles and was called 'Robert of the Ruins.'

exploreAction.targetName: The Bathing Pool (Met, New York) — the ruins
exploreAction.instruction: A grand colonnade in ruin frames a washing day: women scrub linen in a pool where Roman emperors once bathed. Look at the scale — tiny figures, giant columns, ivy reclaiming everything. Robert made time itself the subject: empires pass, laundry continues.

name: Joseph Wright of Derby
teaser: The English painter who made science heroic — his Experiment with an Air Pump shows a family gasping around a demonstration of a vacuum, lit like a Caravaggio with the Enlightenment as its subject. He painted the birth of the industrial age.

exploreAction.targetName: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump (National Gallery, London) — the light
exploreAction.instruction: A philosopher demonstrates a vacuum while the bird inside the glass suffocates — and every face reacts differently: wonder, horror, curiosity, sleep. Look at the candle, the skeleton in the jar, the children. Wright painted the moral cost of knowledge, and it glows.

name: Henry Fuseli
teaser: The Swiss-born painter of nightmares — his The Nightmare, with its crouching incubus and the horse's head at the curtain, terrified and thrilled Europe in 1781. He painted the subconscious a century before Freud gave it a name.

exploreAction.targetName: The Nightmare (Detroit Institute of Arts) — the creature
exploreAction.instruction: A woman sleeps in a tangle of sheets while a demon squats on her chest and a horse's head glows through the curtains. Look at the lighting — theatrical, from nowhere — and the contradiction: it's pornographic, terrifying, and hilarious all at once. Fuseli painted the dream logic you've had.

name: William Blake
teaser: The English poet-painter who saw visions and painted them — his muscular, flaming figures of God, angels, and Newton measure the universe with golden compasses. He invented his own mythology and printed his books by hand, combining image and text like no one before.

exploreAction.targetName: Newton (Tate Britain) — the compass
exploreAction.instruction: Newton leans into a rock of stars, drawing a compass over a scroll — the Enlightenment as a beautiful, terrible act. Look at the muscular body, the seaweed-like hair, the geometry carved into stone. Blake admired Newton's mind and feared where it pointed; he painted both feelings at once.

name: John Martin
teaser: The English painter of apocalyptic spectacle — his vast canvases of the Last Judgment, the Great Day of His Wrath, and cities swallowed by earthquake made Victorian audiences queued in the streets. He painted the end of the world like a blockbuster.

exploreAction.targetName: The Great Day of His Wrath (Tate Britain) — the scale
exploreAction.instruction: Mountains crack, cities crumble, and a wall of fire consumes the world — with tiny human figures for scale. Look at how Martin uses geology as drama: chasms, cliffs, and lightning. He influenced Hollywood's disaster movies a century before they existed.

name: Samuel Palmer
teaser: The English visionary who painted the Kent countryside as a dream of gold — his early 'Shoreham period' works show a moonlit, harvest-rich, Biblical England that he called 'the valley of vision.' His later years were quieter; the early ones are the miracle.

exploreAction.targetName: In a Shoreham Garden (Victoria and Albert Museum) — the gold
exploreAction.instruction: A garden gate, a mass of blossom, a hillside — all rendered in swirling, glowing pigment like stained glass. Look at the intensity: Palmer painted memory, not nature. He said he wanted to paint 'the soul of the scene.' This is a valley seen with a believer's eyes.

name: Richard Parkes Bonington
teaser: The English watercolorist who died at 25 and influenced Delacroix, Constable, and the whole French landscape school — his coastal scenes are loose, luminous, and decades ahead of their time. He painted air itself, before Impressionism existed.

exploreAction.targetName: The Coast of Picardy or his Venice watercolors
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Bonington suggests a whole coastline in a few washes of blue and ochre — no detail, all atmosphere. He worked fast, in the open air, and made the sketch a finished thing. Delacroix said his friend taught him 'the art of the indispensable.'

name: David Wilkie
teaser: The Scottish painter who made village life a national genre — his penny weddings, blind fiddlers, and cottage interiors were the most popular pictures in early 19th-century London. He took Hogarth's storytelling and filled it with warmth.

exploreAction.targetName: The Blind Fiddler (Tate Britain) — the children
exploreAction.instruction: A family in a cottage dances to a blind fiddler while a baby reaches for the coins and a boy imitates the fiddle with a poker. Look at the faces — each one a different delight. Wilkie painted Scotland's kitchens as theaters of ordinary joy, and the royals lined up to buy them.

name: Edwin Landseer
teaser: The Victorian painter of animals with human souls — his dogs, stags, and lions (including the Trafalgar Square lions) were the most beloved images in Britain. The Monarch of the Glen turned a stag into a portrait of noble solitude.

exploreAction.targetName: The Monarch of the Glen (National Galleries of Scotland) — the stag
exploreAction.instruction: A giant stag stands alone in the Highlands, silhouetted against a golden sky. Look at the realism of the fur and antlers — Landseer was also a sculptor who dissected animals to paint them truly. Victoria and Albert loved him; he painted their dogs so well they wept.

name: William Powell Frith
teaser: The Victorian painter of crowds — his Derby Day and Paddington Station crammed thousands of tiny figures, each with a story, into a single canvas, and audiences needed opera glasses to see it all. He was the era's greatest visual storyteller.

exploreAction.targetName: The Derby Day (Tate Britain) — the crowd
exploreAction.instruction: The Epsom Derby in 1856: pickpockets, acrobats, lovers, aristocrats, and a barefoot boy with a giant boot. Look for the details — the stolen watch, the monkey, the carriage of courtesans. Frith painted society as a novel you read with your eyes.

name: Ford Madox Brown
teaser: The English painter who chronicled the industrial age with a Pre-Raphaelite eye — his Work shows a London street where laborers dig a sewer while philosophers, orphans, and a policeman pass, a complete social atlas in one canvas.

exploreAction.targetName: Work (Manchester Art Gallery) — the street
exploreAction.instruction: In the middle, the navvies dig — heroes in their own way — while the idle rich, the starving poor, and the sandwich-board man pass by. Look at the faces: Brown painted his friends into the crowd, and wrote a whole pamphlet explaining every figure. A Victorian allegory in a puddle of mud.
